items.title: Baidu unveils Apollo World, an agent-driven multimodal world model for physical AI, already used in Apollo Go testing
items.original_title: 百度首次披露Apollo World具身世界模型：用AI教AI开车
items.summary: At Baidu AI Day (Apollo session) in Shenzhen on Nov 3, Baidu Apollo first disclosed Apollo World, an agent-driven, all-modality world model for physical AI. Traffic participants in its virtual city are modelled as decision-making AI agents, and it generates camera images and lidar point clouds in real time so a driving system can act and feed back in a closed loop. Baidu proposed a '2+3' test for world models (causality and interactivity as thresholds; physical accuracy, persistence and real-time as advanced metrics) and says the model is already used in Apollo Go (Luobo Kuaipao) global testing and validation, with the stack extensible to robotics.
items.why_it_matters: A simulator that trains and tests driving stacks could cut real-road mileage needs for Baidu's robotaxi expansion, and positions Baidu in the world-model race for physical AI.

items.title: At Wuzhen AI dialogue, DeepSeek, Alibaba Qwen and MiniMax leads debate open-source model risk
items.original_title: 国内三大顶尖大模型负责人乌镇同台对话：开源后如何防范风险
items.summary: On Nov 3 the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit's main forum held its first 'AI Wuzhen Dialogue', moderated by Zhejiang Lab director Wang Jian, with representatives of DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen and MiniMax. DeepSeek research engineer Gao Xi said open-sourcing can amplify AI safety risks and DeepSeek is studying remedies. Qwen LLM project lead Liu Dayiheng said the main open-source risks are irrevocability and lack of external safeguards, argued restricting openness alone will not fix this, and criticised capability-tiered controls as possibly underestimating models. MiniMax's Feng Wen stressed that open models give enterprises with private data control over post-training and fine-tuning.
items.why_it_matters: It shows how China's leading open-model labs publicly frame safety and openness at a state-backed forum, as Beijing's draft AI export controls take aim at model weights.

learn.title: Why a world model's rollout error compounds, and how to measure it
learn.why_today: Baidu's Apollo World is described as a world model for physical AI, and a world model is only useful if its multi-step predictions stay accurate.
learn.explanation: A world model is trained to predict the next state from the current one, usually with teacher forcing: it always sees the true previous state. At use time it must feed on its own predictions, so a small one-step error is re-applied at every step. With an unstable or marginally stable system the error grows roughly geometrically; in this toy, stable dynamics make it saturate instead. The numbers are illustrative and say nothing about Baidu's model. Evaluate with open-loop rollouts at several horizons, not only one-step loss, and consider training on the model's own rollouts to close the gap.
learn.python:
import random
random.seed(0)
# Toy 1-D world model: true dynamics x' = 0.95x + noise; learned model has 3% slope error.
a_true, a_hat = 0.95, 0.98
def rollout(h, trials=2000):
    err = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        x = xh = 1.0
        for _ in range(h):
            x = a_true * x + random.gauss(0, 0.02)
            xh = a_hat * xh           # model feeds on its own predictions
        err += abs(x - xh)
    return err / trials
for h in (1, 5, 20, 50):
    print(h, round(rollout(h), 4))
